title: Project risk and issue management
apm_learning_objective: Understand project risk and issue management in the context of a project.
exam_coverage_note: 8 of 60 marks. Joint second largest objective, alongside scope management.
source_ref: APM PFQ Qualification Handbook, APM-QS-PFQ-8 V5 (April 2026), §11d. Syllabus maps this objective to APM Body of Knowledge 7th ed. 4.2.2, 4.2.3, 4.3.3, 4.3.5 and 8th ed. 5.4.3, 5.10, 5.10.1, 5.10.2, 5.10.3.
competence_area_note: The handbook publishes no per-objective Competence Framework mapping. Left null rather than guessed.
where_this_fits: Eight marks, and the cleanest structure in the syllabus. Four outcomes are about risk, three are about issues, and one asks you to tell them apart. Once you know that an issue has already happened and a risk has not, most of the objective answers itself.

key_definitions.definition: An uncertain event or set of circumstances that, should it occur, would affect the achievement of objectives.
key_definitions.plain_english: Something that might happen and would matter if it did. It has not happened yet.

key_definitions.definition: A problem that has occurred and that requires resolution beyond the delegated authority of the project manager.
key_definitions.plain_english: Something that has already happened, is causing a problem now, and is too big for the project manager to absorb alone.

key_definitions.definition: The process of identifying, analysing and responding to risk throughout the life of a project, to minimise threats and maximise opportunities.
key_definitions.plain_english: Working out what could go wrong or right, how much it would matter, and doing something about it in advance.

key_definitions.definition: A record of identified risks, their assessment, their owners and the planned responses, maintained throughout the project.
key_definitions.plain_english: The live list of risks, who owns each one, and what is being done about it.

key_definitions.definition: The process by which issues are identified, assessed, escalated and resolved so that project objectives can still be achieved.
key_definitions.plain_english: How the project deals with problems that have already landed.

key_definitions.definition: A risk with a negative effect on objectives should it occur.
key_definitions.plain_english: The kind of risk people usually mean when they say risk.

key_definitions.definition: A risk with a positive effect on objectives should it occur.
key_definitions.plain_english: Uncertainty that could work in your favour, and which should be managed rather than left to luck.

core_content.key_takeaway: A risk is an uncertain event or set of circumstances that, should it occur, would affect the achievement of objectives. It has not happened yet, and the moment it does happen it stops being a risk and becomes an issue. A risk can be positive as well as negative: a negative one is a threat and a positive one is an opportunity.
core_content.body_markdown:
Two elements matter.

First, uncertainty. A risk has not happened, and might not. Once it happens it is no longer a risk.

Second, effect on objectives. Something uncertain that would not affect the project's objectives is not a project risk, however interesting it is. The link to objectives is what makes it worth managing.

The part people most often miss is that a risk can be positive. Treating risk as a synonym for bad news loses marks, because half of risk management is about opportunities.

core_content.outcome_title: Explain the purpose of risk management
core_content.key_takeaway: The purpose of risk management is to minimise threats to the project's objectives and to maximise opportunities. Both halves count, and the second is the one people forget. Risk management does not eliminate uncertainty, so any answer promising that is wrong.
core_content.body_markdown:
Both halves are examinable and the second is routinely forgotten. A project that only ever manages downside is doing half the job. If a supplier offers early delivery, or a new tool could cut testing time, those are uncertainties with positive effects and they deserve deliberate management rather than luck.

What risk management does not do is remove uncertainty. Every project is uncertain, because every project is doing something that has not been done in exactly this form before.

The practical purpose is to make uncertainty visible early enough to act cheaply. A risk spotted at concept can be designed out. The same risk discovered during delivery can only be absorbed.

core_content.outcome_title: Outline the stages of a typical risk management process
core_content.key_takeaway: The four stages of a typical risk management process are identification, analysis, response and closure. Identification finds the risks, analysis assesses each one by probability and impact so that attention can be prioritised, response decides and implements what will be done, and closure formally closes risks that can no longer occur. The process is continuous, because new risks appear throughout the project.
core_content.body_markdown:
Take the four stages in turn.

Identification finds the risks. Techniques include workshops, checklists, lessons from previous projects, and structured scans of the outside environment.

Analysis assesses each risk, usually by probability and by impact on objectives, so attention can be prioritised. A risk that is near certain and severe is not managed the same way as one that is remote and trivial.

Response decides and implements what will be done. For threats the options are broadly to avoid, reduce, transfer or accept. For opportunities they are to exploit, enhance, share or reject.

Closure formally closes risks that can no longer occur, because the event has passed or the circumstances have changed. Without closure, registers fill with dead entries and the live risks get lost among them.

core_content.outcome_title: Describe the use of risk registers
core_content.key_takeaway: A risk register records identified risks together with their assessment, their owners and the planned responses. A typical entry has a description of the risk, its probability and impact, the response chosen, the actions agreed, the person who owns it and its current status. It is live, reviewed and updated throughout the project, and the named owner is what makes it a register rather than a list of worries.
core_content.body_markdown:
Ownership is the part that makes the document work. A risk with no named owner is a risk nobody is managing, and a register full of unowned risks is a list of worries. Assigning ownership turns each entry into somebody's responsibility.

The register is live. It is reviewed and updated throughout the project, new risks are added as they emerge, assessments change as circumstances change, and risks that can no longer occur are closed.

It also feeds other things. Progress reporting draws on it, decision gates consider it, and the business case is re-tested against it when major risks change.

core_content.key_takeaway: An issue is a problem that has occurred and that requires resolution beyond the delegated authority of the project manager. Both parts matter. The problem is real and present rather than potential, and it goes beyond what the project manager can decide alone, so it has to be escalated.
core_content.body_markdown:
The first element separates an issue from a risk. The problem is real and present, not potential.

The second element is worth pausing on. Project managers deal with problems constantly, and most of those never become issues in the formal sense, because they sit inside the authority the project manager already holds. An issue is specifically a problem that needs a decision from someone higher up.

Issues arrive from two directions. Some are risks that occurred, which is why the risk register and the issue log are connected. Others simply happen without ever having been foreseen.

core_content.outcome_title: Outline the purpose of issue management
core_content.key_takeaway: The purpose of issue management is to ensure that issues are identified, assessed, escalated and resolved so that the project's objectives can still be achieved. The word is resolution, not prevention. An issue has already happened, so it cannot be prevented, and prevention belongs to risk management.
core_content.body_markdown:
You cannot prevent an issue, because by definition it has already happened. Any answer offering prevention as the purpose of issue management is wrong on the definition alone.

What issue management provides is a route. Without one, a problem beyond the project manager's authority either stalls the project while nobody decides, or gets absorbed quietly by someone acting beyond their authority. Both are worse than escalating it.

Speed matters as much as process. An unresolved issue usually costs more the longer it sits, because work carries on around it and rework builds up.

core_content.outcome_title: Differentiate between an issue and a risk
core_content.key_takeaway: The difference is certainty. A risk is uncertain and lies in the future. An issue has occurred and exists now. Both are recorded, both have owners and both can affect cost, time, quality or scope, and a risk that occurs becomes an issue.
core_content.body_markdown:
Everything people reach for as a difference, other than certainty, is false. Both are recorded. Both have owners. Both can affect cost, time, quality or scope. Both can be escalated. Neither belongs to one type of constraint.

The relationship is worth holding on to: a risk that occurs becomes an issue. Good risk management reduces how many risks make that transition, and prepares a response for those that do.

A short test. Ask whether the thing described has happened. If yes, issue. If not yet, risk. If a question describes something already delaying testing or breaching a tolerance, it is an issue however it is phrased.

core_content.outcome_title: State the stages of an issue resolution process
core_content.key_takeaway: A typical issue resolution process runs: the issue is identified and logged, its impact is assessed, it is escalated to the appropriate level of authority, a resolution is agreed and implemented, and the issue is closed once resolved. There is no probability assessment, because the event has already happened.
core_content.body_markdown:
Take the stages in turn.

The issue is identified and logged, so that it exists as a recorded item with an owner rather than as an escalating conversation.

Its impact is assessed. Because the event is certain, the assessment concerns severity and consequence for the objectives, not likelihood.

It is escalated to the appropriate level of authority. This is the stage that separates issue resolution from routine problem solving.

A resolution is agreed and implemented by whoever holds the authority to decide, and the actions are tracked to completion.

The issue is closed once resolved, and any consequences are reflected in the plan, the baseline or the risk register.

Notice what is absent. There is no probability assessment, because the event has already happened.

misconceptions.wrong: Risk means something bad that might happen.
misconceptions.right: A risk is an uncertain event that would affect objectives. Negative risks are threats, positive ones are opportunities, and both are managed.
It minimises threats and maximises opportunities. Uncertainty is inherent in doing something unique, so it can be managed but never removed.

misconceptions.wrong: Every problem on a project is an issue.
misconceptions.right: An issue is a problem beyond the project manager's delegated authority, requiring escalation. Most day to day problems are handled within tolerance.

misconceptions.wrong: An issue is just a risk that has been recorded.
misconceptions.right: An issue is a risk that has occurred, or a problem that arrived unforeseen. Recording has nothing to do with the distinction.
It resolves them. Stopping things happening is risk management, acting on events that have not occurred.

misconceptions.wrong: An issue can be assessed for probability.
misconceptions.right: It has already happened, so its probability is one. Assessment concerns severity and consequence.

misconceptions.wrong: The risk register is written once during planning.
misconceptions.right: It is live throughout. New risks are added, assessments change, and risks that can no longer occur are formally closed.

memory_aids.expansion: Identification, Analysis, Response, Closure. The four risk management stages named in the syllabus.
Yes means issue. Not yet means risk. The single question behind eight marks.
Risk cuts both ways. If an answer only manages the downside, it is only doing half of risk management.
An issue is certain. Any option assessing its likelihood is wrong by definition.

progress_checkpoint: I can define risk including the words uncertain and objectives, and note that it can be positive.
I can state both halves of the purpose of risk management.
I can name the four stages of the risk management process in order.
I can list what a risk register entry contains, including owner and response.
I can define an issue including the tolerance element, and state the purpose of issue management without using the word prevent.
I can give the one real difference between a risk and an issue, name three false ones, and say why issue resolution has no probability stage.

source_confidence.claim: The four stages of a typical risk management process are identification, analysis, response and closure.
source_confidence.basis: Named in the bracketed 'including' list in syllabus outcome 7.3. The handbook states bracketed content is examinable.

source_confidence.claim: An issue requires resolution beyond the project manager's delegated authority.
source_confidence.basis: Consistent with the APM Body of Knowledge treatment of issue management and with the published sample paper, whose correct answer refers to breaching delegated tolerances.
source_confidence.risk: Everyday usage treats any problem as an issue. Teaching the tolerance element is what separates a correct exam answer from a colloquial one.

source_confidence.claim: Threat responses are broadly avoid, reduce, transfer or accept; opportunity responses are exploit, enhance, share or reject.
source_confidence.basis: Standard APM treatment of risk responses, included as supporting context for the response stage.
source_confidence.risk: The syllabus outcome asks only for the stages of the process, not for the response types. Teach these as context; do not present them as separately examinable at PFQ level.
